statement: Every point of the plane is given a half turn ($180^\circ$) about the point $A(1, 2)$, and then a half turn about the point $B(4, 6)$. Where does the point $P(3, -1)$ end up?

choices.misconception: I did only the first half turn, about A, and forgot to carry out the second one.
I did the half turns in the opposite order, about B first and then about A.
I did only the half turn about B and forgot the first move about A.
I thought two half turns about different points add up to a slide by the vector from A to B, which is (3, 4).

hints: A half turn sends each point straight through the centre to the far side.
A half turn about C makes C the midpoint of a point and its image, so X goes to 2C - X. Apply this rule twice, in the order given.
The half turn about A sends P(3, -1) to (2 - 3, 4 + 1) = (-1, 5). Now give (-1, 5) a half turn about B(4, 6).

solutions.reliable: A half turn about C makes C the midpoint of a point and its image, so $X$ goes to $2C - X$. About $A(1, 2)$: $P(3, -1)$ goes to $(2 - 3, 4 + 1) = (-1, 5)$. About $B(4, 6)$: $(-1, 5)$ goes to $(8 + 1, 12 - 5) = (9, 7)$. The transferable idea: a half turn about C is the rule $X \to 2C - X$, so chains of half turns reduce to simple arithmetic.
solutions.elegant: Two half turns give $2B - (2A - X) = X + 2(B - A)$, a slide by twice the vector from A to B. Here $B - A = (3, 4)$, so every point moves by (6, 8), and P(3, -1) lands on (9, 7).

whyOnTest: Composing half turns tests careful coordinate work and the surprising fact that two half turns make a slide of twice the distance between the centres.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
